# Book III, Proposition 6

*Circles touching one another do not have the same centre*

[Euclid's proof](#euclids-proof) · [In Lean](#in-lean) · [What it rests on](#what-it-rests-on) · [Mishnah](#mishnah)

> If two circles touch one another, they will not have the same centre.

**In Lean:** ✅ proved, as Euclid states it · Euclid's argument · two of our tacit rules together already contain it (see Overlap)

## Euclid's proof

<p align="center"><img src="../../figures/III/06.svg" alt="Euclid's figure for Proposition III.6, with Heath's letters. Drawn for one case: the circles touching within, as in Heath's figure. Like Heath's, this figure draws the impossible supposition: F as one centre of ABC and CDE, two circles that touch." width="360"></p>

<p align="center"><em>Drawn for one case: the circles touching within, as in Heath's figure. Like Heath's, this figure draws the impossible supposition: F as one centre of ABC and CDE, two circles that touch.</em></p>

For let the two circles ABC, CDE touch one another at the point C;

I say that they will not have the same centre.

For, if possible, let it be F; let FC be joined, and let FEB be drawn through at random.

Then, since the point F is the centre of the circle ABC,

FC is equal to FB.

Again, since the point F is the centre of the circle CDE,

FC is equal to FE.

But FC was proved equal to FB;

therefore FE is also equal to FB, the less to the greater: which is impossible.

Therefore F is not the centre of the circles ABC, CDE.

Therefore etc.

Q. E. D.

From [`Elements/BookIII/Prop06.lean`](../../Elements/BookIII/Prop06.lean). Euclid's sentences are the `--` comments, and our own notes are in `/- … -/`; the lines under each sentence are the Lean that carries it out. The list below marks where a lemma does a step Euclid takes for granted, where several sentences share one step and where the Lean takes a case Euclid's figure leaves aside; the `/- … -/` notes in the listing explain smaller adjustments.

**How the Lean follows the text**

- **A further case.** "For, if possible, let it be F…" Contact without, which Euclid leaves to the reader, ends here: F would be within both circles, as a centre is within its circle, and circles touching without have no point within both. Euclid's argument then runs for contact within, either circle the inner.
- **Done by `Tacit.circle_eq`.** "therefore FE is also equal to FB, the less to the greater…" That E and B are two points is the step Euclid leaves tacit: were they one, the circles, about the one centre F, would be one circle (System E, Diagram-segment 2), and circles touching within are two. Then whichever of E and B is the nearer F gives the less, as in his figure, where E is.
- **Carried together.** "Therefore F is not the centre of the circles ABC, CDE." The reductio's conclusion. The Lean supposed F the centre of both circles at the start and has reached a contradiction in each kind of contact: at once for contact without, and by Euclid's argument for contact within.

```lean
/-- If two circles touch one another, they will not have the same centre. -/
theorem Prop6 {C F : Point} {ABC CDE : Circle} (htouch : CirclesTouch ABC CDE C) :
    ¬ (Centre F ABC ∧ Centre F CDE) := by
  -- For let the two circles ABC, CDE touch one another at the point C;
  have hC : OnCircle C ABC ∧ OnCircle C CDE := by
    rcases htouch with ⟨h₁, h₂, -⟩ | ⟨h₂, h₁, -⟩ | ⟨h₁, h₂, -⟩ <;> exact ⟨h₁, h₂⟩
  -- I say that they will not have the same centre.
  -- For, if possible, let it be F; let FC be joined, and let FEB be drawn through at random.
  rintro ⟨hF₁, hF₂⟩
  /- Contact without, which Euclid leaves to the reader, ends here: F would be within
     each circle, as a centre is (`centre_inside`), and circles touching without have no
     point within both. So the circles touch within, whichever is the inner, and are two. -/
  have hne : ABC ≠ CDE := by
    rcases htouch with ⟨-, -, hne, -⟩ | ⟨-, -, hne, -⟩ | ⟨-, -, hout⟩
    · exact hne
    · exact hne.symm
    · exact absurd (centre_inside hF₂) (hout F (centre_inside hF₁))
  /- FC is drawn for the eye; our proof uses only its ends. An unlettered point
     chooses the direction of FEB, which meets both circles beyond F. -/
  obtain ⟨X, hX⟩ := exists_point [F]
  have hXF : X ≠ F := fun h => hX (h ▸ List.mem_singleton_self F)
  obtain ⟨L, hF_L, hX_L⟩ := Postulate1 F X hXF.symm
  obtain ⟨B, hB, hB_L, hBFX⟩ := line_circle_beyond (centre_inside hF₁) hF_L hX_L hXF
  obtain ⟨E, hE, hE_L, hEFX⟩ := line_circle_beyond (centre_inside hF₂) hF_L hX_L hXF
  -- Then, since the point F is the centre of the circle ABC,
  -- FC is equal to FB.
  have hFB : ‖F C‖ = ‖F B‖ := Definition15 hF₁ hC.1 hB
  -- Again, since the point F is the centre of the circle CDE,
  -- FC is equal to FE.
  have hFE : ‖F C‖ = ‖F E‖ := Definition15 hF₂ hC.2 hE
  -- But FC was proved equal to FB;
  -- therefore FE is also equal to FB, the less to the greater: which is impossible.
  have hEB : ‖F E‖ = ‖F B‖ := hFE.symm.trans hFB
  /- That E and B are two points is the step Euclid leaves tacit, as in III.5. Were they
     one, the circles, about the one centre F, would pass through one point and be one
     circle (`circle_eq`); but circles touching within are two. -/
  have hEB_ne : E ≠ B := by
    rintro rfl
    exact hne (circle_eq hF₁ hF₂ hB hE rfl)
  /- E and B both lie beyond F from the unlettered point, so B is on the ray from F
     through E, and only one point of a ray is at a given distance from its start
     (`OnRay.eq_of_len_eq`, as in III.5): whichever is the nearer, the less would be
     equal to the greater. Euclid's figure has E the nearer. -/
  have hB_ray : OnRay B F E := ⟨(ne_of_between hEFX).symm, ne_of_between hBFX,
    ⟨L, hF_L, hE_L, hB_L⟩,
    not_between_of_between_between (between_symm hBFX) (between_symm hEFX)⟩
  exact hEB_ne (OnRay.eq_of_len_eq hB_ray hEB.symm).symm
  -- Therefore F is not the centre of the circles ABC, CDE.
  -- Therefore etc.
  -- Q. E. D.
```

## Mishnah

_Our commentary: what Euclid assumes, what Lean made us say out loud, and how the result looks by modern means._

**"Let FEB be drawn through at random."** Euclid supposes that two touching circles have one centre, F, and lets the point of contact, C, settle it. FC is a radius of both circles. A straight line drawn from F at random, FEB, reaches the inner circle at E before the outer at B, and yet FE and FB would each be equal to FC: "the less to the greater: which is impossible".

**"To the intelligence of the reader."** Euclid's figure shows the circles touching within, and the English editions say "internally" in the enunciation, a word Heath calls an interpolation. The fact is, he writes, that "in his usual manner, he chose for demonstration the more difficult case, and left the other case (that of *external* contact) to the intelligence of the reader. It is indeed sufficiently self-evident that circles touching externally cannot have the same centre; but Euclid's proof can really be used for this case too" (vol. 2, p. 13). We take him at his word: our statement covers circles touching within, whichever is the inner, and circles touching without.

**Must E and B be two points?** J. G. Camerer thought the proof takes for granted what Euclid proves only in III.13, that circles touching within at C meet nowhere else. Heath answers that "it is only necessary that *one* line drawn from the assumed common centre should meet the circles in different points" (vol. 2, p. 13). Our proof answers as Heath does, for every straight line from F: were E and B one point, the circles would be one (`circle_eq`, as in III.5), and circles touching within are two. Contact without ends sooner, before FEB is drawn: the common centre would be a point within both circles, and by Definition III.3, which we take to mean the whole circles (see III.11), circles touching without have none.

**The modern way.** Circles of radii R and r that touch have their centres R + r apart if they touch without, and |R − r| apart if they touch within, where R ≠ r, since two circles of one radius cannot touch within. Neither distance is zero, so the centres differ.

## Further reading

- For the test of the modern way, centres R + r apart for circles touching without and R − r for circles touching within, Roger A. VI, "Tangent Circles", §152 (p. 110), an elementary treatise on the triangle and the circle, now free to read, that begins where Euclid's circles leave off.
